title: AI and the Judiciary
lead: In ==June 2026== the SC's AI Committee released draft ==‘Regulations for Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Courts, 2026’== for public consultation — signalling that the judiciary itself now recognises ==AI governance as unfinished business== that must be settled ==before, not after==, deeper adoption.
intro: “Technology as an enabler of justice, not a substitute for judgement” — the guiding philosophy repeatedly invoked by the Government and the Supreme Court.

sections.title: Why the Judiciary Cannot Ignore AI

items: ==Access to justice== — backlogs, cost and language barriers keep the poor and rural population outside the practical reach of courts.
==Capacity constraints== — with ==a fifth to a quarter of sanctioned posts vacant==, human resources alone cannot clear the backlog.
==Administrative overload== — judges spend disproportionate time on scheduling, records and research: tasks that ==don't require judicial mind application== but consume judicial bandwidth.
==Global competitiveness== — contract-enforcement rankings track dispute-resolution speed; AI efficiency has a ==direct economic dividend==.
==Irreversibility of early choices== — the architecture decided now will be very hard to reverse once AI is embedded: ==a decisive constitutional moment==.

items.title: Existing Bodies
bullets: ==SC e-Committee== — policy and strategy for court digitisation under e-Courts Phases I–III; HCs implement with local adaptation
==SC AI Committee== — chaired by a sitting SC judge; oversees translation, research assistance, process automation; ==authored the 2026 Draft Regulations==
Sub-committees of HC judges and technical experts on ==secure connectivity, authentication and protection of judicial data==

items.title: Constitutional & Legal Anchors
bullets: ==Art 21== — speedy trial and access to justice justify efficiency-enhancing technology
==Arts 141 & 145== — binding decisions and rule-making power give the SC the basis to frame AI regulations
==DPDP Act, 2023== intersects wherever litigant/case data is processed — though courts largely sit outside its direct enforcement architecture
==Funding==: e-Courts Phase III outlay of ==₹7,210 crore== with a specific ==‘Future Technological Advancement’== component for AI, ML and blockchain

head: Body
Composition / role
rows: Sitting SC and HC judges, a MeitY official, finance and cybersecurity experts, advocates — ==sets national standards, approves AI systems, publishes annual governance reports==.
Framed under the Apex Body; oversee adoption within their jurisdiction.
A ==District Judge-level officer== in each court for day-to-day operational governance.
Judicial; Technical; Infrastructure & Finance; Case & Data Management; ==Cyber Security==.
Centre of Research and Excellence on AI — a ==neutral research body==: evaluates tools, maintains a central registry and technical standards, advises the Apex Body, ==with no procurement stake==.

items.title: What Is Permitted
bullets: Case management, ==transcription, translation, legal research, summarisation==, accessibility, court administration
Lawyers may use AI in drafting pleadings — subject to ==mandatory disclosure== of the AI-assisted character (==Regulation 43==)
Where AI ==‘materially assists’== a judge, courts must ==inform litigants and counsel== in a timely, accessible manner
Private vendors only with ==written approval== and mandatory contract terms on ==data ownership and IP==

items.title: What Is Absolutely Prohibited
bullets: ==Risk-scoring for flight risk==
==Predicting recidivism==
==Evaluating bail eligibility== through AI
==Determining credibility== of witnesses, parties, accused or counsel
==Predicting, profiling or inferring future conduct== of any party
Submitting AI-generated output as ==independent evidence==, or without disclosure
==‘Black-box’ (unexplainable) systems== in matters affecting personal liberty

items: ==Conflict of interest== — the Apex Body regulating AI in courts is appointed predominantly by sitting judges of the ==same judiciary it oversees==.

==Fragmented standards== — no uniform mandatory technical benchmarks (error rates, explainability thresholds, training-data provenance), so ==each of 25 High Courts may set different approval standards== → inconsistent justice.
==Disclosure burden== — ==SCAORA has opposed== the blanket AI-disclosure requirement (Reg 43) as unworkable against existing professional-conduct norms.
==Capacity gap== — in-house audit duties and a bar on sharing source code presuppose technical capacity most courts don't have.
==Interface with the national AI-governance framework== (MeitY guidelines) remains undefined.

items.title: Structural & Institutional
bullets: ==Fragmented governance== — each wave of court technology spawned separate committees, fragmenting accountability
==No permanent execution body== — unlike ==NPCI for UPI== or ==UIDAI for Aadhaar==, the judiciary lacks a permanent, resourced institution with continuity

items.title: Standards & Accountability
bullets: ==Absence of uniform technical standards== — what must be explained, to whom, and what error rate is tolerable in a bail matter vs scheduling
==Standard-setter/procurer overlap== — unless CoRE-AI is genuinely free of procurement interest
==Explainability and the ‘black box’ problem== — in tension with due process

items.title: Bias, Fairness & Rights
bullets: ==Algorithmic bias== — historical data encodes caste, religion, gender and economic bias; illustrated by the ==COMPAS recidivism controversy== in the US
==Fair trial and natural justice== — outsourcing evidentiary, bail or sentencing logic to opaque algorithms dilutes ==audi alteram partem==
==Digital divide== — efficiency for e-filing and virtual hearings can disadvantage litigants without literacy, devices or connectivity

items.title: Data, Security & Capacity
bullets: Judicial data is ==highly sensitive== — ownership, retention, vendor access, cross-border flows; ==DPDPA interface unsettled==
==Cybersecurity risk== grows with every AI touchpoint in ICMIS/CIS
Wide variation in ==digital literacy== across 25 HCs and thousands of subordinate courts
==Vendor dependency== — IP claims over tools built on judicial data create ==lock-in==
==Overburdened existing bodies== with rotating memberships lack permanence

head: Country / region
Initiative
rows: ==Smart Courts== (since 2016); Shanghai's ‘206’ system; Hangzhou Internet Court's ==Xiao Zhi==
Judicial guidance permitting AI for ==summarisation/administrative tasks only==
==2024 Guidelines for Use of AI in Canadian Courts== (Canadian Judicial Council)

items.title: Institutional Reform
bullets: ==Consolidate the fragmented committee architecture== into a single, permanent, adequately staffed institution — on the ==UIDAI/NPCI== model
==Insulate CoRE-AI== from procurement and vendor relationships — the ==UPI-style separation== of standard-setter from market participant
Address conflict of interest by including ==independent technologists, civil society and bar representatives== in the Apex Body

items.title: Standards & Safeguards
bullets: ==Notify uniform mandatory technical standards== — error rates by use-case, explainability requirements, training-data provenance
==Mandate algorithmic audits and bias-testing== disaggregated across caste, gender, religion and region, with ==published audit summaries==
==Retain and strengthen the non-derogable prohibitions== on bail, recidivism, witness-credibility and black-box liberty uses

items.title: Access, Capacity & Inclusion
bullets: ==Scale multilingual and voice tools== (SUVAS, PANINI, ASR-SHRUTI) to ==district and taluka courts==, not just the SC and HCs
==Digital literacy training== for judges, staff and legal-aid lawyers — paired with continued ==offline access== (e-Seva Kendras, DLSAs)
Extend AI-assisted guidance (==Singapore Small Claims== model) to ==Lok Adalats, Gram Nyayalayas and consumer fora==

items.title: Data, Law & Rollout
bullets: A ==specific judicial-data protection protocol==
==Contractually bar vendors from IP claims== on models trained on judicial data; mandate ==data localisation and access logging==
Place core prohibitions and the Apex Body's mandate on a ==statutory footing== (legislation or Art 145 rules) for durability beyond one CJI's tenure
==Periodic parliamentary and public reporting== for democratic accountability
==Phased, evidence-based rollout== — pilots with transparent criteria and ==sunset/review clauses==
==Recurring consultation cycles== with litigants, the Bar and civil society
